guides.title: How a Two-Stroke Engine Works
guides.summary: The mechanism of the two-stroke engine from first principles: crankcase compression, port timing, scavenging, the tuned expansion chamber, lubrication and fuelling, the diesel and direct-injection variants, and the failure modes that define how these engines are run and repaired.

sections.heading: What a Two-Stroke Engine Is and Where You Meet It
sections.body:
A two-stroke engine completes a full working cycle in one revolution of the crankshaft, which means every downward movement of the piston is a power stroke. A four-stroke engine takes two revolutions to do the same job, dedicating separate strokes to intake, compression, power and exhaust. That single structural difference produces everything else about the two-stroke: its power density, its simplicity, its characteristic noise, its appetite for oil, and its emissions problem. 

The consequence people notice first is power for weight. In principle an engine that fires twice as often at the same speed should make twice the power from the same displacement. In practice a well-developed crankcase-scavenged two-stroke makes something closer to one and a half times the power of an equivalent four-stroke, because getting the burnt gas out and the fresh charge in during the small window around bottom dead centre is imperfect and some of the fresh mixture escapes. Even so, a 250 cubic centimetre motocross two-stroke of the 1990s produced roughly the same output as a 400 to 450 cubic centimetre four-stroke while weighing considerably less. 

The second consequence is mechanical simplicity. A classic small two-stroke has three moving parts: the piston, the connecting rod and the crankshaft. There is no camshaft, no valve train, no timing chain or belt, no oil pump, no sump. Because there is no sump of liquid oil relying on gravity, the engine will run in any orientation, upside down included, which is precisely why chainsaws, brushcutters, hedge trimmers and leaf blowers were built this way for decades. Fewer parts also means lower cost and easy field repair. 

You still meet two-strokes across a wide range of machines. Handheld garden and forestry equipment remains a stronghold, though four-stroke and battery alternatives have taken much of it. Outboard motors, snowmobiles and personal watercraft use large, often direct-injected two-strokes. Off-road motorcycles, trials bikes and karts use them for the power-to-weight advantage. Small generators, water pumps, model aircraft engines and older mopeds and scooters are two-stroke. At the opposite extreme of size, the largest and most thermally efficient internal combustion engines ever built, the low-speed marine diesels that drive container ships, are also two-strokes, though they work on a rather different principle from the small petrol engines. Road-going two-stroke motorcycles and cars have almost entirely disappeared from regulated markets, for reasons rooted in the same scavenging compromise that gives the engine its power. 

A note on names helps early. Two-stroke and two-cycle mean the same thing. Crankcase-scavenged describes the simple petrol engine that uses the underside of its own piston as the charging pump; blower-scavenged describes the larger engines, almost all diesels, that use a separate pump or turbocharger and keep a conventional oil-filled crankcase. The two families share a cycle and almost nothing else, which is the source of much confusion about whether two-strokes are dirty and inefficient or the most efficient engines ever built. Both claims are true, of different machines.

sections.heading: The Four-Stroke Comparison and Why Two Strokes at All
sections.body:
To see what the two-stroke is trading, it helps to lay the two cycles side by side. A four-stroke engine takes the piston down to draw in air and fuel through a valve, up to compress it, down again after ignition to deliver power, and up once more to push the burnt gas out through another valve. Four piston strokes, two crankshaft revolutions, one power stroke. Each of the four jobs gets a whole stroke of roughly 180 degrees of crank rotation to itself, so each can be done thoroughly, and the intake and exhaust events are controlled by valves whose timing can be chosen independently. 

The two-stroke has to fit all four jobs into two strokes. It does this by overlapping them. The upward stroke performs compression above the piston while simultaneously drawing fresh mixture into the crankcase below it. The downward stroke delivers power above the piston while compressing the fresh mixture in the crankcase below. Near the bottom of the stroke, exhaust and intake happen together through openings in the cylinder wall, in a window of perhaps 120 to 140 degrees of crank rotation shared between them. Every event is compressed in time, and two events that a four-stroke keeps strictly separate, the removal of burnt gas and the admission of fresh charge, now happen at the same moment in the same space. 

That overlap is the central compromise. Because burnt gas and fresh charge share the cylinder simultaneously, some fresh mixture inevitably follows the exhaust out of the port, a loss called short-circuiting or scavenging loss. In a simple carburetted two-stroke the escaping fraction may be twenty to forty per cent of the delivered charge depending on load and speed, and since the mixture contains fuel, that fuel is thrown away unburnt. It is simultaneously a fuel-economy penalty, a hydrocarbon-emissions disaster and the reason a two-stroke smells the way it does. 

Against that sits a real list of advantages. Twice the firing frequency gives smoother torque delivery per cylinder and allows a lighter flywheel. There is no valve train to absorb power, wear out or limit engine speed. Manufacturing is cheap. The engine is light, compact and orientation-independent. Cold starting is easy because compression is modest. And because the crankcase is a pump rather than an oil reservoir, the whole bottom end can be small. Whether the trade is worth making depends entirely on the application, which is why two-strokes have survived exactly where their advantages are decisive and disappeared where regulation has made the scavenging loss unacceptable. 

There is also a durability difference that follows from arithmetic rather than poor engineering. A two-stroke's bearings take a firing load twice as often, and its oil arrives once and leaves rather than being filtered and recirculated. That is why a small two-stroke may need attention after a few hundred hours where a four-stroke runs for thousands, and why it is nevertheless cheap to rebuild when it does.

sections.heading: The Cycle Step by Step
sections.body:
Follow one full revolution of a simple crankcase-scavenged two-stroke, starting with the piston at the bottom of its travel. The cylinder wall carries openings: an exhaust port on one side, transfer ports on the other side or sides, and, in the simplest layout, an inlet port lower down. The piston itself acts as the sliding valve that opens and closes them, so the timing of every event is fixed by where the ports are cut and how tall the piston is. 

As the piston rises from bottom dead centre it first covers the transfer ports, then the exhaust port. From the moment the exhaust port closes, the charge above the piston is genuinely trapped and true compression begins. This is why two-strokes have two compression ratios that must not be confused. The geometric ratio, measured from bottom dead centre, might be 12 or 13 to one; the trapped ratio, measured from exhaust port closure, is typically only 7 to 9 to one, and the trapped figure governs detonation and the octane needed. Meanwhile the rising piston enlarges the crankcase and creates a partial vacuum, the inlet opens, and fresh air and fuel rush in from the carburettor. 

Just before top dead centre the spark fires, typically 15 to 30 degrees early depending on speed and design. The charge burns, pressure rises to perhaps 40 to 60 bar, and the piston is driven down. Below it the descending crown shrinks the crankcase, closing the inlet and compressing the fresh charge trapped there to only 1.3 to 1.5 bar absolute. The crankcase is not a combustion space; it is a low-pressure pump whose effectiveness depends on being small, sealed and unobstructed. 

About 80 to 100 degrees before bottom dead centre the descending piston uncovers the exhaust port. Cylinder pressure is still well above atmospheric, so burnt gas blows down rapidly on its own, an event called blowdown that lasts only a few crank degrees but does most of the work of emptying the cylinder. Some 55 to 65 degrees before bottom dead centre the transfer ports open, and the pressurised charge in the crankcase flows up into the cylinder, pushing the remaining exhaust gas ahead of it. The piston reaches bottom dead centre, begins to rise, closes the transfers and then the exhaust, and the cycle repeats. One revolution, one power stroke, and every port timing symmetrical about bottom dead centre because a piston edge cannot be in two places at once. 

Two points deserve emphasis. The window for emptying and refilling is remarkably short: at 6,000 revolutions per minute the crankshaft turns 36 degrees per millisecond, so a transfer period of 120 degrees lasts a little over three milliseconds, and everything about port shape and pipe design exists to make that work. And the crankcase and cylinder are two gas spaces working half a revolution out of phase, connected only through the transfers, so a two-stroke is best pictured as a pump and an engine stacked vertically on one piston.

sections.heading: Crankcase Compression: The Piston as a Pump
sections.body:
The defining feature of the small two-stroke is that the crankcase is a pump. In a four-stroke the crankcase is a large, vented, oil-filled space whose volume changes hardly matter. In a two-stroke it is a sealed chamber whose volume is deliberately made as small as possible, so that the piston's movement produces a useful pressure swing. This arrangement, patented by the English engineer Joseph Day in 1891 and simplified by his employee Frederick Cock to use the piston skirt itself as the inlet valve, is what made the two-stroke cheap enough to become ubiquitous. Dugald Clerk had built working two-stroke engines from about 1878, but they used a separate charging cylinder and were not simple. 

Because the pump is a fixed-volume displacement device, its efficiency depends on a quantity called the crankcase compression ratio: the crankcase volume with the piston at top dead centre divided by its volume at bottom dead centre. Values around 1.4 to 1.5 to one are typical. Raising it increases the pressure available to drive the transfer flow, which helps at low speed, but reduces the volume actually delivered and can hurt at high speed, so it is a tuning variable. Filling unnecessary volume with stuffer plates or with fuller crank webs is a standard way to raise it. 

Because the crankcase must hold pressure, the seals matter enormously. A two-stroke depends on tight crankshaft seals at each end, a sound base gasket, an intact cylinder base and an unwarped mating face. A leak in any of them lets air in on the vacuum part of the cycle without fuel, leaning the mixture; because the oil arrives dissolved in the fuel, a leaner mixture also means less oil. A crankcase air leak is therefore the single most common cause of an otherwise healthy two-stroke overheating and seizing, and it is the first thing an experienced mechanic checks when a small engine will not idle, hunts in speed, or runs hot despite correct jetting. 

Three arrangements control the flow into the crankcase. Piston-port induction uses the piston skirt as the valve; it is the simplest and cheapest, but its timing is necessarily symmetrical, so it must open early and close late, and at low speed some charge blows back out of the carburettor. Reed-valve induction places a one-way petal valve of thin steel or composite between carburettor and crankcase, which closes automatically whenever crankcase pressure rises and so eliminates blowback and broadens the usable speed range. Rotary disc valve induction mounts a slotted disc on the crankshaft end, giving fully asymmetric and freely chosen timing at the cost of a wider engine and a carburettor mounted on the side of the crankcase; it was favoured by Kawasaki and by Rotax in kart and aircraft engines.

sections.heading: Ports Instead of Valves
sections.body:
A two-stroke replaces the four-stroke's poppet valves with holes cut through the cylinder wall, opened and closed by the moving piston. The consequences of that substitution run through the whole design. Because the piston edge passes each port twice per revolution, once going down and once coming up, every piston-controlled port timing is necessarily symmetrical about bottom dead centre. If the exhaust opens 85 degrees before bottom dead centre it must close 85 degrees after it. There is no way to make the exhaust close earlier than it opened without adding another device, and that single geometric fact drives an enormous amount of two-stroke engineering. 

Port timing is quoted either in crank degrees or as a port height above the top of the piston at bottom dead centre, and the two are related through the crank throw and rod length. Typical values for a road two-stroke are an exhaust port opening 80 to 90 degrees before bottom dead centre, giving a duration of 160 to 180 degrees, and transfer ports opening 55 to 62 degrees before, giving 110 to 124 degrees. A high-output racing engine may run 95 degrees or more of exhaust timing, which yields large peak power over a narrow band and very little below it. Raising the exhaust port by even half a millimetre moves the whole power curve upward in engine speed and takes torque away from the bottom, which is why milling the cylinder base or skimming the head changes an engine's character so dramatically. 

Port area matters as much as timing. The total window area available at any crank angle determines how fast gas can move, and designers characterise it with a figure called specific time-area, the integral of port area over the open period divided by swept volume. Ports are made wide rather than tall to gain area without extending duration, but a port that is too wide relative to the bore, beyond roughly 70 per cent of bore width for a single exhaust port, will let a piston ring bulge into it and snap. That is why wide exhaust ports are bridged with a central pillar, and why transfer ports come in multiples. 

Port shape controls direction. The transfer passages are angled deliberately, both upward and toward the cylinder wall opposite the exhaust, so the entering charge follows a designed path. Their upper edges are the steering surfaces, and altering them changes scavenging quality far more than making them bigger. Two further details follow from having holes in the bore. Piston rings must be prevented from rotating, or their ends will catch a port edge, so two-stroke rings are located by a small pin pressed into the ring groove. And the bore surface must tolerate the ports' sharp edges without wearing, which is why hard chrome and nickel-silicon carbide plating, commonly called Nikasil, replaced cast iron liners in high-performance two-strokes: those coatings can be applied to an aluminium cylinder that also conducts heat away from the exhaust bridge far better than iron would.

sections.heading: Scavenging: Emptying and Filling at the Same Time
sections.body:
Scavenging is the process of replacing burnt gas with fresh charge, and it is the two-stroke's central engineering problem, because both happen through open ports at the same time. The quality of scavenging determines how much fresh mixture stays in the cylinder, how much burnt gas remains to dilute it, and how much fresh mixture escapes down the exhaust pipe. Engineers describe the outcome with two ratios: delivery ratio, the mass supplied compared with a full cylinder, and trapping efficiency, the fraction of that supply which actually stays. 

Three geometries have been used. Cross scavenging, the oldest, places the transfer ports directly opposite the exhaust port and fits the piston with a raised deflector on its crown to turn the incoming charge upward so it does not run straight across and out. It is simple, and it dominated small engines and outboards for decades, but the deflector piston is heavy, awkward to cool and produces a poor combustion chamber shape, and mixing losses are high. 

Loop scavenging, patented by Adolf Schnürle in Germany in the mid-1920s and licensed widely from DKW onward, is the arrangement used in essentially all modern petrol two-strokes. Two or more transfer ports are placed on either side of the exhaust port and angled so their streams converge on the cylinder wall opposite the exhaust, turn upward together, travel across the cylinder head and come back down toward the exhaust port, sweeping the burnt gas ahead of them in a loop. Because the fresh charge takes the long way round, the piston crown can be flat and light, and trapping efficiency is markedly better. Practical designs add a third boost port between the transfers, opposite the exhaust, angled steeply upward, and five-port and seven-port cylinders are common. 

Uniflow scavenging is the most effective of all and is used where the extra complexity pays. Air enters through a ring of ports all around the bottom of the cylinder, often given a swirl by angling them tangentially, and leaves through one or more poppet valves in the cylinder head. The gas therefore moves in one direction only, from bottom to top, and mixing between fresh and burnt gas is minimal. This is the layout of the Detroit Diesel two-strokes and of every large marine low-speed diesel. Older opposed-piston designs, such as the Junkers Jumo aircraft diesels and the Napier Deltic, achieved uniflow with two pistons per cylinder running toward each other and no cylinder head at all. Because uniflow engines cannot fill the cylinder using crankcase pumping alone, they need a blower or turbocharger, and in the Detroit Diesel that Roots blower is the source of the engine's distinctive scream. The general ranking is consistent: cross scavenging is cheapest and worst, loop scavenging is the best that can be done with crankcase pumping and no head valves, and uniflow is the best available at the cost of needing a separate air pump and a valve train.

sections.heading: The Expansion Chamber: Sound Waves as a Valve
sections.body:
The symmetry problem created by piston-controlled ports has one elegant solution, and it is the reason a tuned two-stroke sounds and behaves as it does. Since the exhaust port cannot be made to close early, the exhaust system is used to push the escaped charge back in before it does. The device that does this is the expansion chamber: a pipe that widens into a diverging cone, runs through a parallel belly section, then narrows again through a converging cone into a small outlet called the stinger. 

The physics is pressure-wave reflection. When the exhaust port opens, a sharp positive pressure pulse travels down the pipe at the local speed of sound. In exhaust gas at roughly 600 degrees Celsius that speed is around 590 metres per second, considerably faster than in cool air, and it varies with temperature, which matters later. When the pulse reaches the diverging cone it meets an expanding area, and a pressure wave reflecting from an area increase returns inverted, as a negative or rarefaction wave. That suction wave arrives back at the exhaust port while the transfers are open, and it actively pulls burnt gas out of the cylinder and draws fresh charge up through the transfer ports far more vigorously than crankcase pressure alone could. 

The same pulse continues down the pipe and meets the converging cone, an area decrease, from which a wave reflects without inversion, as a positive pressure wave. If the pipe's lengths are chosen correctly, that positive wave arrives back at the exhaust port in the few degrees between the transfers closing and the exhaust closing, and it stuffs the fresh charge that had escaped back into the cylinder. The net effect is a cylinder filled to more than atmospheric pressure. Delivery ratios above one are routinely achieved, which is why a tuned 125 cubic centimetre racing two-stroke could reach specific outputs above 200 horsepower per litre without forced induction. 

The technique was developed to its modern form by Walter Kaaden, chief engineer at MZ in East Germany, during the late 1950s, working with limited resources and building on earlier German work on the exhaust pulse. When the MZ rider Ernst Degner defected to the West in 1961, taking the knowledge with him to Suzuki, the technology spread rapidly through Japanese racing. The cost is bandwidth. Wave travel time is fixed by the pipe's geometry and the speed of sound in the gas, but the time available is set by engine speed, so the returning wave arrives at the right moment only over a narrow band, typically a few thousand revolutions per minute wide. Below it the positive wave arrives too late and does nothing; above it the wave arrives too early and pushes back against the outgoing exhaust. That is the two-stroke powerband, an abrupt surge of torque whose edges a rider learns to feel, and it also explains why a cold pipe, whose gas is denser and slower, shifts the tuned speed downward until the engine warms.

sections.heading: Lubrication and Fuel Mixing
sections.body:
A two-stroke has no oil sump, because the crankcase is a pump handling fresh charge. Lubrication is therefore a total-loss system: oil is carried into the engine dissolved in the fuel or metered into the intake, coats the crankshaft bearings, connecting-rod bearings, piston skirt and cylinder wall on its way through, and is then burnt or blown out of the exhaust. Nothing is recirculated, nothing is filtered, and the oil supply is proportional to fuel flow, which is a reasonable proxy for load. 

Premix ratios are quoted as parts of fuel to one part oil. Modern equipment with good synthetic oil commonly specifies 50 to 1, which is two per cent oil; 40 to 1 and 32 to 1 are common on older or harder-worked machines; 25 to 1 and 20 to 1 appear on vintage engines and some racing applications where mineral or castor-based oils are used. The manufacturer's figure is not a suggestion. Too little oil starves the bearings and seizes the engine; too much displaces fuel, richens combustion, fouls plugs, cokes the exhaust port and increases smoke. Oils are graded against published standards, most usefully the Japanese JASO FC and FD ratings for low smoke and detergency in air-cooled engines and the marine NMMA TC-W3 rating for water-cooled outboards; a TC-W3 oil is formulated for lower operating temperatures and is not a substitute in a chainsaw. 

Oil-injection systems, introduced on production motorcycles by Yamaha as Autolube in the mid-1960s and by Suzuki soon afterward, meter oil from a separate tank with a small pump driven by the engine and linked to the throttle, so the ratio varies with load rather than staying fixed. This gives less oil at idle and cruise and more at full throttle, reducing smoke and plug fouling. The failure mode is silent: if the pump, its cable or the oil supply fails, the engine runs perfectly on straight petrol until it seizes, which is why many owners of injected machines add a small amount of premix as insurance or convert to premix outright.
ingredients: Fresh unleaded petrol of the octane the manufacturer specifies, bought in small quantities; petrol begins to lose light fractions and form gum within about thirty days in a vented container, and stale fuel is the commonest cause of small-engine no-starts.
A two-stroke oil carrying the rating the machine calls for, typically JASO FC or FD for air-cooled handheld equipment and NMMA TC-W3 for water-cooled outboards; these are not interchangeable.

A calibrated mixing container or a graduated measure, so the ratio is measured rather than estimated; at 50 to 1, five litres of petrol takes 100 millilitres of oil, and at 32 to 1 it takes about 156 millilitres.
A clean, sealable, approved fuel can, filled only part way if the mix will be stored, and labelled clearly with the ratio and the date it was mixed.

Fuel stabiliser if the mix will sit longer than a month, and ethanol-free petrol where it is available, since ethanol attracts water, can separate in storage and attacks older rubber fuel lines and diaphragms.

sections.heading: Fuelling and Ignition
sections.body:
Most two-strokes have been fuelled by a carburettor, a device that uses the pressure drop of air accelerating through a restriction, the venturi, to draw fuel from a reservoir through calibrated jets. In a small engine the carburettor must work across an enormous range of conditions with no electronics, so it is divided into overlapping circuits. A pilot or idle circuit, fed by a small jet and adjusted by an air or fuel screw, supplies the engine at closed throttle. The needle, a tapered rod attached to the throttle slide, controls the middle range, and moving the clip on it up or down changes mixture from roughly a quarter to three quarters throttle. The main jet governs full throttle. The slide cutaway influences the transition just off idle. Handheld equipment usually uses a diaphragm carburettor instead of a float bowl, so it can run at any angle: a rubber diaphragm sensing crankcase pulses works a fuel pump, and a second diaphragm and needle valve maintain the metering chamber at constant pressure. 

Carburettor tuning is temperature and altitude sensitive because the jets meter fuel by volume while the engine breathes air by mass. Air density falls roughly ten per cent for every thousand metres of altitude and also falls as temperature rises, so an engine jetted at sea level on a cold morning will run rich on a hot day in the mountains. Racers routinely rejet for conditions, and the practical rule is that a rich two-stroke runs cooler, smokier and duller while a lean one runs hotter, sharper and toward seizure. 

Ignition on a small two-stroke is normally self-powered, which is why a chainsaw needs no battery. Magnets set into the flywheel rim sweep past coils on a stator plate, generating current directly. Older systems used contact breaker points, a mechanical switch opened by a cam on the crankshaft, which collapsed the field in an ignition coil and fired the plug; points wear, pit and drift out of adjustment, and their gap sets the timing. Since the 1970s capacitor discharge ignition has replaced them: a charge is stored in a capacitor and dumped through the coil primary by a thyristor triggered electronically, giving a hotter, faster spark and timing that can be varied with engine speed by the ignition module. 

Ignition timing is expressed in degrees before top dead centre and is a compromise. More advance gives the charge time to burn and raises peak pressure, but too much causes the pressure rise to fight the still-rising piston and promotes detonation. Two-strokes generally run less advance at high speed than one might expect, often retarding above the powerband, because the pipe is stuffing extra charge in and cylinder pressure is already high. The spark plug's heat range is a related and frequently misunderstood variable: it describes how quickly the plug conducts heat away, not how hot the spark is. Too cold a plug fouls with oil and carbon at light load, too hot a plug becomes an ignition source and causes pre-ignition, and reading the colour of the insulator and the strap remains a genuinely useful diagnostic.

sections.heading: Power Valves and Variable Exhaust Timing
sections.body:
The narrow powerband of a tuned two-stroke follows directly from two fixed compromises: exhaust port timing must be symmetrical, and the expansion chamber is tuned for one engine speed. A tall exhaust port and a racing pipe give large peak power and almost nothing below it. A short port and a mild pipe give usable torque everywhere and a modest peak. From the early 1980s manufacturers found ways to change the exhaust timing while the engine was running, which recovered much of the low-speed torque without giving up peak power. 

The most common approach is a movable blade or guillotine that slides down across the top of the exhaust port at low engine speed, lowering its effective roof and shortening the duration, then withdraws above a threshold to expose the full port height. Yamaha's Power Valve System, introduced on production road bikes in 1982, works this way. Honda's version used a rotating cylindrical valve across the port roof; KTM, Kawasaki and others developed their own. Actuation is usually mechanical, by a centrifugal governor driven off the crankshaft pulling a cable, or by a servo motor under electronic control, and the valve is often designed to open progressively over a band of a few thousand revolutions per minute rather than snapping open. 

A second family of devices changes the effective volume rather than the timing. Small auxiliary chambers alongside the exhaust port, opened at low speed and closed at high speed, alter the acoustic length and volume that the pressure wave sees, effectively retuning the pipe. Rotax's system on kart and snowmobile engines works this way, and several manufacturers combine both approaches. Variable-geometry pipes with sliding sections exist but are rare, because a moving joint in hot, oily exhaust is hard to seal. 

Power valves work, and a modern motocross two-stroke with one is far more tractable than an equivalent engine without, but they also introduce the most common maintenance item on such engines. The valve sits in the hottest, dirtiest part of the exhaust tract, and the carbon deposited there by burnt two-stroke oil progressively gums the mechanism until the valve sticks. A stuck-closed valve produces an engine that pulls cleanly from low speed and then refuses to rev out; a stuck-open valve produces one with no bottom end that comes alive only at high speed. Both symptoms are diagnostic, and periodic cleaning of the valve and its linkage with solvent and a soft scraper is routine work rather than a repair. 

It is worth being clear about what a power valve does not do. It does not change the expansion chamber's tuned speed, which stays fixed by the pipe's geometry, so a power-valve engine still has a distinct powerband; what the valve adds is usable torque below it. Nor does it substitute for correct jetting or a sound crankcase. An engine flat everywhere has a fuelling or sealing problem, and the diagnostic distinction is that a valve fault shows as a sharp change in character at one engine speed rather than as general dullness.

sections.heading: Direct Injection and the Modern Clean Two-Stroke
sections.body:
The two-stroke's fatal emissions problem is not combustion but scavenging: fresh mixture containing fuel escapes unburnt through the exhaust port. If the fuel is not in the cylinder while the exhaust port is open, that loss disappears entirely. Direct injection does exactly this, spraying fuel straight into the cylinder after the exhaust port has closed, so only air and oil mist are lost during scavenging. The idea is old; making it work in a cheap engine took decades, because the injector must deliver a finely atomised, correctly shaped spray in the very short time between port closure and ignition, at engine speeds up to several thousand revolutions per minute. 

Two production approaches solved it. Air-assisted direct injection, developed by the Orbital Engine Company in Australia under Ralph Sarich from the 1980s, uses a small engine-driven air compressor. Fuel is first metered into a chamber by a conventional low-pressure injector, then blown into the cylinder by a burst of compressed air through a second injector at around 6 to 8 bar. The air shears the fuel into a very fine mist and carries it in a controlled plume. Mercury's OptiMax outboards used this licensed technology. High-pressure single-fluid injection dispenses with the compressor and uses a fuel injector capable of very rapid opening at much higher pressure; Ficht injection, introduced by Outboard Marine Corporation in the 1990s, used an electromagnetically driven plunger, and after severe early reliability problems the concept was refined by Bombardier into the Evinrude E-TEC engines. 

The gains are substantial and well documented. Direct-injected two-stroke outboards cut hydrocarbon emissions by roughly seventy-five to ninety per cent against the carburetted engines they replaced, improved fuel consumption by around thirty to forty per cent at cruise, and allowed oil consumption to be reduced because lubricant could be metered independently of fuel, often at effective ratios beyond 100 to one at light load. They also retained the two-stroke's light weight, low parts count and strong low-speed torque, which is why they remained competitive against four-stroke outboards rather than being displaced entirely. 

Direct injection also enables stratified charge operation at light load, where a small quantity of fuel is injected late and concentrated near the spark plug in a cloud of otherwise very lean air. That allows the engine to run at overall air-fuel ratios far leaner than would burn if the mixture were uniform, cutting pumping and heat losses. The remaining obstacles to direct injection in very small handheld engines are cost and the need for electrical power and control electronics, which is why chainsaws and trimmers have mostly gone a different route, using stratified scavenging in which a charge of pure air is admitted above the fuel-air mixture in the transfer passages, so that clean air rather than mixture is what escapes first.

sections.heading: Two-Stroke Diesels, from Truck to Container Ship
sections.body:
Compression-ignition two-strokes are a different machine from the small petrol engine, and understanding why clarifies the whole subject. A diesel injects fuel directly into the cylinder near top dead centre, long after the ports have closed. Only air is being pumped through the cylinder during scavenging, so no fuel is lost, and the two-stroke's greatest weakness simply does not exist. What remains is its greatest strength: a power stroke every revolution. 

Because they scavenge with air alone and use uniflow layouts, these engines cannot rely on crankcase pumping; they need an external air supply. The Detroit Diesel 71 series, introduced in 1938 and named for its 71 cubic inches of displacement per cylinder, used a Roots blower to force air through a ring of ports at the bottom of each liner, with poppet exhaust valves in the head, and became one of the most widely produced engines of the twentieth century in trucks, buses, boats and generators. Its characteristic sound comes from the blower and from firing every revolution. The Napier Deltic, an opposed-piston design with three banks arranged in a triangle and eighteen cylinders, powered British locomotives and fast patrol boats and remains a notable example of the opposed-piston uniflow idea. 

At the largest scale the two-stroke diesel is not merely competitive but dominant. The low-speed crosshead engines built by MAN and by Wärtsilä-Sulzer that drive large ships are two-strokes with uniflow scavenging, one hydraulically actuated exhaust valve per cylinder, and turbochargers driven by exhaust energy. Because a propeller is most efficient turning slowly, these engines are designed to run at 60 to 120 revolutions per minute and connect directly to the shaft with no gearbox. The Wärtsilä-Sulzer RTA96-C, in its fourteen-cylinder form, has a bore of 960 millimetres, a stroke of 2,500 millimetres and delivers around 80,000 kilowatts, roughly 107,000 horsepower. Its brake thermal efficiency exceeds fifty per cent, which makes it the most efficient single-cycle heat engine ever built. 

Several features make that efficiency possible. The very long stroke gives a high expansion ratio and a low mean piston speed, which reduces friction. The crosshead arrangement, in which a guide takes the side thrust so the piston rod stays axial, allows the combustion space to be completely separated from the crankcase, so cylinder lubrication and crankcase lubrication use different oils and the crankcase oil stays clean. Firing every revolution means each cylinder produces its power with less peak stress for a given output. Modern versions replace the camshaft with electronically controlled hydraulic actuation of injection and the exhaust valve, allowing timing to be optimised continuously across the load range. The engines burn heavy residual fuel oil, historically the cheapest liquid fuel available, though sulphur limits imposed by international regulation from 2020 have pushed operators toward low-sulphur fuels, scrubbers and dual-fuel gas operation.

sections.heading: Cooling, Materials and Wear
sections.body:
A two-stroke fires twice as often as a four-stroke of the same size and speed, so it puts roughly twice as much heat into the same amount of metal, and it does so without the four-stroke's cooling intake stroke of pure air and without a circulating oil system to carry heat away from the piston underside. Thermal management is therefore a first-order design problem rather than an afterthought. 

Air-cooled engines rely on fins whose area, spacing and airflow are carefully worked out, and they are vulnerable in ways owners often overlook: a chainsaw whose cooling fins are packed with sawdust, or a scooter whose fan shroud has been removed for appearance, will overheat regardless of how well it is jetted. Liquid-cooled two-strokes gain much closer control of metal temperature, which lets designers run tighter piston clearances and higher outputs, and they dominate motocross, road racing and outboard applications. Even then, the exhaust bridge, the narrow pillar of metal dividing a wide exhaust port, is the hottest place in the cylinder and the usual origin of a scuffed bore, which is why it is often drilled for oil or given extra clearance on the piston. 

Material choices follow from heat and from the presence of ports. Early cylinders were cast iron, which is tough and cheap but a poor conductor. Modern high-output cylinders are aluminium with a hard plating bonded directly to the bore: hard chrome, or more commonly a nickel matrix carrying dispersed silicon carbide particles, sold under names such as Nikasil and its many equivalents. These coatings are only some 0.05 to 0.15 millimetres thick, cannot be rebored, and are replated or replaced when worn, which changes the economics of rebuilding. Pistons are cast or forged aluminium alloy, usually with high silicon content to reduce thermal expansion, running clearances of the order of 0.05 to 0.10 millimetres depending on size and cooling. 

Wear in a two-stroke is dominated by the total-loss lubrication and by the ports. Because oil arrives with the fuel and is burnt, bearing life depends directly on mixture strength, and lean running is a lubrication problem as much as a heat problem. Big-end and main bearings are normally roller or needle types rather than plain shells, because a total-loss oil film cannot support a hydrodynamic plain bearing reliably. Ring life is short compared with a four-stroke because rings pass over port edges thousands of times a minute, and carbon builds steadily in the exhaust port, the power valve and the head of the pipe. Decarbonising, once a routine seasonal chore on every two-stroke, remains necessary: a heavily coked exhaust port loses effective area and timing, and the loose carbon flakes it eventually sheds can jam a ring or score a bore.

sections.heading: Emissions and the Regulatory Squeeze
sections.body:
The two-stroke's decline in regulated markets was not a matter of fashion. A carburetted crankcase-scavenged engine loses a substantial fraction of its fresh charge straight out of the exhaust port, and because that charge contains fuel, the resulting hydrocarbon emissions are very high. Measurements through the 1980s and 1990s repeatedly found small two-strokes emitting unburnt hydrocarbons at levels tens of times those of comparable four-strokes, and a widely cited comparison found that operating certain older two-stroke garden equipment for an hour produced hydrocarbon emissions comparable to driving a modern car for hundreds of kilometres. Total-loss lubrication compounds it, since some of the oil passes through unburnt as visible smoke and fine particulate. 

There is one genuine emissions advantage worth stating fairly. Because a two-stroke retains a good deal of burnt gas in the cylinder, an effect equivalent to heavy exhaust gas recirculation, peak combustion temperatures are lower and nitrogen oxide formation is correspondingly reduced. That has never been enough to offset the hydrocarbon and particulate problem in petrol engines, though it is one reason large two-stroke diesels behave better on nitrogen oxides than their size might suggest. 

Regulation closed in from several directions. In the United States, Environmental Protection Agency rules on small spark-ignition engines from the late 1990s, tightened in successive phases, and California's stricter Air Resources Board standards forced redesign or withdrawal of most carburetted handheld two-strokes. A 1996 outboard rule requiring a roughly seventy-five per cent reduction in hydrocarbon emissions over a decade effectively ended the conventional carburetted two-stroke outboard and drove the industry to direct injection and to four-strokes. In Europe, successive emission standards for motorcycles and mopeds from the late 1990s onward made the road-going two-stroke uneconomic, and the last mainstream two-stroke road motorcycles left European showrooms early in the 2000s. India, which had enormous two-stroke scooter and rickshaw fleets, moved decisively to four-strokes over the same period on urban air-quality grounds. 

The engineering responses have been real rather than cosmetic. Direct injection removed the fuel from the scavenging loss entirely. Stratified scavenging, in which a layer of clean air is introduced ahead of the fuel-air charge so that air rather than mixture is what escapes, cut hydrocarbon emissions in handheld equipment by well over half at modest cost and is now standard on many chainsaws and trimmers. Catalytic converters have been fitted to small two-strokes, though the oil in the exhaust shortens their life. Where none of these was economic, the engine simply lost, which is why the two-stroke now survives in a smaller and more specialised set of applications than it occupied in 1980, alongside a growing displacement of handheld equipment by battery electric motors that have no emissions problem at all at the point of use.

sections.heading: Running, Tuning and Routine Maintenance
sections.body:
A two-stroke rewards a specific set of habits and punishes their absence quickly. Its lubrication depends on the fuel it is drinking at that moment and its cooling is marginal at full load, so most of the discipline concerns heat and mixture. Warm the engine before working it hard, because the piston expands faster than the cylinder and a cold engine at full throttle has the smallest clearance it will ever have. Do not run it at sustained high speed with no load, since fuel flow and therefore oil delivery do not match the heat being generated. Avoid prolonged idling, which cools the plug and fouls it. And let a hard-worked engine idle briefly before shutting down so heat can move out of the piston crown. 

Diagnosis on these engines is unusually tractable, because there are only three requirements for a two-stroke to run: compression, a spark at the right time, and fuel of the right mixture arriving through a sealed crankcase. Almost every fault reduces to one of those, and each can be tested directly with simple equipment.
steps: Check the fuel first. Drain anything over a month old, confirm the mix ratio and that oil was added, and confirm the tank vent breathes; a blocked vent gives an engine that runs two minutes and dies.

Test compression with a gauge through the plug hole at full throttle, pulling until the needle stops rising. A healthy small engine reads roughly 100 to 160 pounds per square inch depending on design; below about 90 it will start poorly or not at all.

Check for spark by earthing the plug against the cylinder and pulling the starter in shade. A weak orange spark that vanishes under compression usually means a failing coil or module rather than a bad plug.
Inspect the spark plug's insulator. Light tan is correct; wet and black is rich or oil-fouled; white, blistered or with a melted strap indicates lean running and dangerous heat.

Pressure and vacuum test the crankcase. With the exhaust and intake sealed by plates, pressurise to about 0.4 bar, roughly 6 pounds per square inch, and confirm it holds for at least ten minutes; then pull a similar vacuum. Pressure leaks find bad gaskets, vacuum leaks find failing crank seals.

Remove the exhaust and look through the exhaust port at the piston and bore with the piston at bottom dead centre. Vertical scoring on the exhaust side is the signature of overheating; scoring on the transfer sides suggests dirt ingestion past the air filter.
Clean or replace the air filter, and check the exhaust port and power valve for carbon, scraping with a plastic or wooden tool and never steel, which gouges the bore plating.

Set carburettor mixture screws to the manufacturer's baseline turns out from lightly seated, then adjust the idle circuit warm, aiming for the highest steady idle and then enriching slightly from that point.
After a rebuild, run in with a richer mixture and several heat cycles of light load, avoiding sustained full throttle for the first few tanks so the rings bed without glazing the bore.

sections.heading: Failure Modes and What They Tell You
sections.body:
The characteristic two-stroke failure is seizure, in which the piston expands or scuffs until it binds in the bore, and the engine stops abruptly. It has several distinct causes with distinguishable evidence, and reading that evidence matters, because rebuilding an engine without finding the cause simply schedules the next seizure. 

A lean seizure is the classic. Too little fuel means too little oil and a hotter, faster burn, so the piston crown and the exhaust side of the skirt overheat, expand and pick up material from the bore. The evidence is heavy vertical scoring concentrated on the exhaust side, a piston crown that may be eroded or holed, and a spark plug that was white or blistered. Its causes are a crankcase air leak, a blocked or too-small main jet, a restricted fuel supply, an air leak at the inlet manifold, or simply running at high altitude on sea-level jetting. A cold seizure produces scoring on all four sides of the piston at once, because the piston expanded while the cylinder was still cold and clearance vanished uniformly; it is a symptom of working the engine hard before it is warm. A dirt-ingestion failure shows scratching concentrated on the intake and transfer sides and points at a damaged or badly fitted air filter. 

Detonation and pre-ignition are related but not identical, and both destroy pistons. Detonation is the spontaneous auto-ignition of the last part of the charge after the spark has fired, producing a sharp pressure wave that hammers the piston crown; it sounds like a metallic rattle under load and leaves a sandblasted, pitted appearance around the crown edge and sometimes broken ring lands. Its causes are too little octane, too much ignition advance, too high a trapped compression ratio, carbon deposits raising compression, and overheating. Pre-ignition is worse: something in the chamber, typically an overheated plug electrode, a glowing carbon flake or a sharp edge, ignites the charge before the spark, so the piston is fighting a rising fire for much of its upward travel. It melts a hole through the crown, often near the exhaust side, in seconds. 

Other failures follow their own signatures. A broken ring end almost always means a ring rotated because its locating pin came loose, or that a port was too wide. A big-end failure produces a knock that worsens with load and metallic debris in the crankcase, and it is frequently the delayed consequence of an earlier oil-starvation episode. A power valve stuck by carbon produces an engine that suddenly cannot rev out or has lost its bottom end. A collapsed or dented expansion chamber changes wave timing and flattens the powerband. The general rule when a two-stroke goes wrong is to be suspicious of anything that could make it lean, since leanness is simultaneously an ignition-timing problem, a heat problem and a lubrication problem, and to fix the cause before the symptom: replace the crank seals, not only the piston.

guides.safetyNote: Two-stroke fuel is a flammable liquid whose vapour ignites easily; mix and store it outdoors in an approved container away from ignition sources. Exhaust contains carbon monoxide and unburned hydrocarbons and must never be run in an enclosed space. Disconnect the spark plug lead before working on any engine with an exposed chain, blade or propeller, and never test compression or spin an engine with the plug removed near fuel vapour.

guides.title: The Otto Cycle Explained
guides.summary: A complete explanation of the four-stroke spark-ignition cycle, from its thermodynamic derivation and efficiency equation through real-engine combustion, knock, valve timing and losses, to diagnosis and the cycle's practical limits.

sections.heading: What the Otto Cycle Is and Why It Matters
sections.body:
The Otto cycle is the thermodynamic description of what happens inside an ordinary petrol engine. It is the
idealised sequence of compression, ignition, expansion and heat rejection that a spark-ignition engine
approximates, and it is the reason a car engine has the shape, the compression ratio, the fuel requirement and
the efficiency that it does. Somewhere close to a billion engines running on this cycle exist on the planet, in
cars, motorcycles, chainsaws, generators, outboard motors, lawnmowers and light aircraft. If you want to
understand why petrol has an octane rating, why an engine has a rev limit, why compression ratios cluster
between about 9 and 13 to one, or why a hybrid engine is tuned differently from a sports engine, the answer in
every case runs through this cycle.

It is important from the start to be clear about what kind of thing the Otto cycle is. It is a model, not a
machine. The model describes a fixed mass of air being compressed, having heat added to it instantaneously at
constant volume, expanding, and then having heat removed at constant volume, all without friction and without
heat leaking through the walls. No real engine does this. A real engine breathes in fresh air and fuel, burns
that fuel over a finite time while the piston is moving, loses a large fraction of the released heat into the
cylinder walls and the exhaust, and pushes the products out through valves against a pressure difference. The
model is nonetheless enormously useful, because it isolates the single dominant variable, the compression ratio,
and shows exactly how it governs the ceiling on efficiency. Everything a real engine does is best understood as
a departure from this baseline.

The core insight the cycle delivers can be stated in one line: efficiency depends on how much you squeeze the
gas before you burn it, and on nothing else in the ideal case. Squeeze harder and a larger fraction of the
released heat becomes work rather than being thrown out of the exhaust pipe. This is a purely thermodynamic
result, not an engineering opinion, and it explains why a century and a half of engine development has consisted
largely of a struggle to raise the compression ratio and of finding ways to stop the fuel exploding when you do.

The cycle also matters historically. The four-stroke engine gave the nineteenth century a compact, self-contained
prime mover that did not need a boiler, a firebox, a water supply or a stoker, and that could be started in
seconds. That combination is what made personal road transport, aviation and mechanised agriculture possible.
Even as electric drivetrains take a growing share of transport, hundreds of millions of Otto-cycle engines
remain in service, and the cycle continues to define the reference point against which alternatives are
measured. Understanding it is a genuine piece of general technical literacy.

sections.heading: Otto, Beau de Rochas and the Birth of the Four-Stroke
sections.body:
Nikolaus August Otto was born in 1832 in Holzhausen an der Haide in what is now Germany, and worked as a
travelling salesman before becoming interested in the noisy, inefficient gas engines of Étienne Lenoir, which
appeared around 1860. Lenoir's engine drew in a mixture of coal gas and air, ignited it partway through the
stroke without any prior compression, and converted perhaps four percent of the fuel's energy into work. Otto's
central intuition, which he pursued for over a decade, was that compressing the mixture before ignition would
transform the result.

In 1864 Otto formed a partnership with Eugen Langen, an engineer and sugar-industry entrepreneur, creating the
firm N. A. Otto & Cie, later the Gasmotoren-Fabrik Deutz and eventually Deutz AG, which survives today. Their
first commercial success, in 1867, was an atmospheric engine in which the explosion drove a piston upward and
useful work was extracted as atmospheric pressure pushed it back down. It won a gold medal at the Paris
Exposition of 1867 and was substantially more economical than Lenoir's design, but it was tall, slow and
limited to a few horsepower.

The breakthrough came in 1876, when Otto built the first practical engine that compressed the charge before
ignition and completed its work in four piston strokes. Working with an initial output on the order of three
horsepower at roughly 180 to 250 revolutions per minute, it achieved around 14 percent thermal efficiency,
several times better than anything before it, and it ran smoothly enough to be marketed as the Otto Silent
Engine. Deutz sold thousands. Two of the engineers who worked there, Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach, would
leave to build the high-speed petrol engines that made the motor car possible.

The intellectual credit is genuinely contested, and it is worth stating the complication honestly. In 1862 a
French engineer, Alphonse Beau de Rochas, had filed a patent describing the four-stroke principle and,
crucially, articulating the conditions for efficiency: the largest possible cylinder volume with the smallest
possible surface, the greatest possible expansion, and the highest practicable pressure at the start of
expansion. Beau de Rochas never built a working engine and his patent lapsed for non-payment of fees, but its
existence was used in litigation, and in 1886 a German court invalidated Otto's key patent on the grounds of
this prior publication. The fairest summary is that Beau de Rochas described the cycle and Otto made it work,
which in engineering is usually the harder half.

The name attached to the thermodynamic cycle reflects that practical achievement. When engineers later
formalised the idealised air-standard analysis, they named it after the man whose engine had demonstrated that
compression before ignition was the decisive move.

sections.heading: Heat Engines and the Thermodynamic Foundations
sections.body:
Before the cycle can be analysed, three ideas from thermodynamics need to be in place, because every subsequent
result follows from them.

The first is the first law of thermodynamics, which is conservation of energy applied to systems that exchange
heat and work. For a closed system the change in internal energy equals heat added minus work done by the
system, written as delta-U equals Q minus W. Internal energy is the energy stored in the random motion of the
molecules, and for an ideal gas it depends only on temperature. This is why a gas that is heated at constant
volume, doing no work because nothing moves, converts every joule of heat into a temperature rise, and why the
relationship for that case is Q equals m times cv times delta-T, where cv is the specific heat capacity at
constant volume, roughly 0.718 kilojoules per kilogram per kelvin for air near room temperature.

The second is the ideal gas law, PV equals mRT, where R for air is 0.287 kilojoules per kilogram per kelvin. It
ties the three state variables together, so that fixing any two fixes the third. Air at ordinary engine
conditions behaves close enough to ideal for this to be a good approximation, though it degrades at the extreme
pressures and temperatures reached just after combustion.

The third is the concept of an isentropic process, meaning one that is both adiabatic, exchanging no heat with
its surroundings, and reversible, involving no friction or turbulence. For an ideal gas, an isentropic process
obeys P times V to the power gamma equals a constant, where gamma is the ratio of specific heats, cp divided by
cv, about 1.4 for air at moderate temperature. From this follow the two working relations used constantly in
engine analysis: temperature ratio equals volume ratio to the power gamma minus one, and pressure ratio equals
volume ratio to the power gamma. Compress air tenfold isentropically and its absolute temperature rises by a
factor of ten to the power 0.4, which is about 2.51.

Finally, the second law of thermodynamics sets the ceiling. No cyclic heat engine can convert all the heat it
receives into work; some must be rejected to a colder reservoir. The theoretical maximum, the Carnot efficiency,
is one minus the ratio of the absolute cold temperature to the absolute hot temperature. With combustion
temperatures around 2500 kelvin and ambient around 300 kelvin, that ceiling is roughly 88 percent, which tells
you immediately that the loss in a real engine is not primarily a second-law inevitability but an engineering
shortfall. The Otto cycle sits well below Carnot because its heat addition and rejection happen across large
temperature differences rather than isothermally, and real engines sit well below the Otto ideal for reasons of
friction, heat transfer, finite burn duration and breathing.

sections.heading: The Air-Standard Otto Cycle: Four Idealised Processes
sections.body:
The air-standard Otto cycle strips a real engine down to a fixed mass of air trapped in a cylinder, undergoing
four processes in sequence and returning to its starting state. The word closed matters: no gas enters or leaves
the model, so intake and exhaust do not appear at all. The heat that combustion would release is instead added
externally, and the heat that leaving exhaust gas would carry away is instead removed externally. This is what
allows the cycle to be treated as a genuine closed thermodynamic loop.

Process one to two is isentropic compression. The piston rises from bottom dead centre to top dead centre,
reducing the volume from V1 to V2, with no heat entering or leaving. Pressure rises as the volume ratio to the
power gamma and temperature rises as the volume ratio to the power gamma minus one. This is the process that
does the work that makes the whole cycle efficient, and it is paid for by the crankshaft, drawing on the
flywheel's stored energy and on the other cylinders.

Process two to three is constant-volume heat addition. In the ideal model, all the heat is added while the
piston is momentarily stationary at top dead centre, so the volume does not change and no work is done. Pressure
and temperature therefore leap together in exact proportion, since at constant volume pressure is proportional
to absolute temperature. This instantaneous addition is the single most severe idealisation in the model, since
real combustion takes tens of crankshaft degrees, but it is also what makes the analysis tractable and what
gives the Otto cycle its formal name, the constant-volume cycle.

Process three to four is isentropic expansion, the power stroke. The high-pressure, high-temperature gas pushes
the piston from top dead centre back to bottom dead centre, expanding through exactly the same volume ratio it
was compressed through. Because pressure during expansion is much higher than during compression at every
corresponding volume, the work extracted here greatly exceeds the work spent on compression, and the difference
is the useful output.

Process four to one is constant-volume heat rejection. The remaining heat is removed at bottom dead centre,
dropping pressure and temperature back to the starting condition and closing the loop. In a real engine this
step corresponds physically to opening the exhaust valve and blowing the hot gas out, which is why an engine's
exhaust is hot and why a substantial fraction of the fuel energy leaves that way regardless of how well the
engine is built.

Because both heat transfers happen at constant volume, both are computed as cv times the relevant temperature
difference, and this is what makes the efficiency expression collapse to something remarkably simple.

sections.heading: Reading the Pressure-Volume and Temperature-Entropy Diagrams
sections.body:
Two plots carry almost all the intuition an engineer needs about this cycle, and learning to read them is worth
more than memorising formulae.

The pressure-volume diagram puts cylinder volume on the horizontal axis and pressure on the vertical. The Otto
cycle traces a shape rather like a distorted teardrop. Starting at bottom right, at large volume and low
pressure, the compression curve sweeps up and to the left, steepening as it goes because pressure varies as
volume to the negative gamma power. At the left-hand extreme, the smallest volume, the constant-volume heat
addition appears as a vertical line shooting upward. The expansion curve then sweeps down and to the right,
sitting above the compression curve all the way. Finally a vertical line drops back down at maximum volume.

The single most useful property of this diagram is that area equals work. The area under any curve on a
pressure-volume plot is the integral of pressure with respect to volume, which is exactly mechanical work. The
area under the expansion curve is the work the gas does on the piston; the area under the compression curve is
the work the piston does on the gas; and the enclosed area between them is the net work produced per cycle. This
is not an analogy, it is the definition, and it is why James Watt's engine indicator, a device that mechanically
drew this diagram on a card from a running steam engine, was such a jealously guarded commercial secret in the
1790s. Engineers still call a measured pressure-volume trace an indicator diagram, and dividing the enclosed
area by the swept volume gives the indicated mean effective pressure, a single number expressing how hard the
engine works each cycle regardless of its size.

The temperature-entropy diagram is less familiar but more revealing about efficiency. Entropy goes on the
horizontal axis, absolute temperature on the vertical. Here the two isentropic processes become perfectly
vertical lines, since entropy does not change, while the two constant-volume processes become curves sloping
upward to the right. Area on this diagram equals heat, so the area under the heat-addition curve is the heat in,
the area under the heat-rejection curve is the heat out, and the enclosed area is again the net work.

What the temperature-entropy plot shows immediately is why the cycle falls short of Carnot. A Carnot cycle is a
rectangle: all heat enters at one high temperature and leaves at one low temperature. The Otto cycle instead
adds heat over a wide temperature range, from perhaps 750 to 2000 kelvin, and rejects it over another wide
range. Every joule added at a temperature below the peak, and every joule rejected at a temperature above
ambient, is a lost opportunity. Raising the compression ratio narrows this gap by pushing the whole heat-addition
curve upward.

sections.heading: Compression Ratio and the Efficiency Equation
sections.body:
The compression ratio is defined geometrically, not thermodynamically: it is the cylinder volume when the piston
is at bottom dead centre divided by the cylinder volume when it is at top dead centre. Writing the swept or
displacement volume as Vd and the clearance volume remaining above the piston at the top as Vc, the ratio r
equals Vd plus Vc, all divided by Vc. A 500 cubic centimetre cylinder with a 50 cubic centimetre combustion
chamber has a compression ratio of 11 to 1. Note what this means physically: the clearance volume is small, so
small changes in it, from a skimmed cylinder head, a thinner head gasket or a different piston crown, move the
ratio noticeably.

The efficiency of the ideal cycle can now be derived in a few lines. Heat in is cv times the difference between
T3 and T2. Heat out is cv times the difference between T4 and T1. Thermal efficiency is work divided by heat in,
which equals one minus heat out divided by heat in, giving one minus the quantity T4 minus T1, divided by the
quantity T3 minus T2. Both isentropic processes run through the same volume ratio, so T2 divided by T1 equals r
to the power gamma minus one, and T3 divided by T4 equals the same quantity. Substituting and cancelling
produces the celebrated result: efficiency equals one minus one divided by r raised to the power gamma minus
one.

This equation deserves to be stared at, because of what it does not contain. It contains no fuel property, no
peak temperature, no engine speed, no cylinder size, no amount of heat added. In the ideal air-standard model,
two engines with the same compression ratio have the same thermal efficiency whether one is a lawnmower and the
other a racing engine, and adding more fuel produces more power at exactly the same efficiency. Only the
compression ratio and the working fluid's gamma appear.

The numbers matter. With gamma at 1.4, a compression ratio of 6 gives 51 percent, 8 gives 56 percent, 10 gives
60 percent, 12 gives 63 percent, 15 gives 66 percent and 20 gives 69 percent. Two features stand out
immediately. First, the ideal figures are far above what real engines achieve, which are typically 25 to 40
percent, so the gap between ideal and real is where nearly all engineering effort lives. Second, the returns
diminish sharply. Going from 8 to 10 buys about four percentage points; going from 16 to 18 buys about one and a
half. Since the mechanical and thermal penalties of high compression rise steeply, there is a practical optimum
well below the theoretical maximum.

Gamma matters too, and it is not really 1.4 inside an engine. Hot combustion products with carbon dioxide and
water vapour have gamma closer to 1.25 to 1.30, which alone cuts the ideal efficiency substantially. This is one
reason lean-burn engines, whose excess air keeps gamma higher, gain efficiency beyond what the compression ratio
alone would predict.

sections.heading: A Worked Example in Numbers
sections.body:
Abstract relationships become concrete quickly when actual numbers are pushed through them, so consider a single
cylinder operating on the ideal air-standard Otto cycle with a compression ratio of 10 to 1. Take conditions at
the start of compression as 100 kilopascals and 300 kelvin, use air properties with gamma equal to 1.4, cv equal
to 0.718 kilojoules per kilogram per kelvin and R equal to 0.287 kilojoules per kilogram per kelvin, and suppose
combustion adds 800 kilojoules of heat per kilogram of air.

Compression first. The temperature ratio is r to the power gamma minus one, that is 10 to the power 0.4, which
is 2.512. So the temperature at the end of compression, T2, is 300 multiplied by 2.512, giving 754 kelvin, a rise
of 454 kelvin achieved purely by squeezing, with no fuel burned at all. This is worth pausing on, because it is
the mechanism behind both diesel ignition and petrol knock. The pressure ratio is 10 to the power 1.4, which is
25.12, so P2 is 2512 kilopascals, roughly 25 atmospheres.

Heat addition next. At constant volume the temperature rise is heat divided by cv, that is 800 divided by 0.718,
which is 1114 kelvin. So T3 equals 754 plus 1114, or 1868 kelvin. Since volume is unchanged, pressure scales with
absolute temperature, so P3 equals 2512 multiplied by 1868 divided by 754, which is about 6225 kilopascals,
around 62 atmospheres. Real petrol engines see peak pressures in this general region, commonly 50 to 90 bar,
which is why connecting rods and main bearings are as substantial as they are.

Expansion follows the same isentropic relation in reverse. T4 equals 1868 divided by 2.512, which is 744 kelvin.
That is the temperature of the gas at the moment the exhaust valve would open, and it explains why exhaust
manifolds glow.

Now the accounting. Heat rejected is cv multiplied by T4 minus T1, that is 0.718 multiplied by 444, giving 319
kilojoules per kilogram. Net work is heat in minus heat out, 800 minus 319, which is 481 kilojoules per kilogram.
Thermal efficiency is 481 divided by 800, which is 0.602, or 60.2 percent, exactly matching the formula one
minus one over 10 to the power 0.4.

One more quantity is worth computing. The specific volume at state one is R times T1 divided by P1, that is
0.287 multiplied by 300 divided by 100, giving 0.861 cubic metres per kilogram, and at state two it is one tenth
of that, 0.0861. The mean effective pressure is net work divided by the swept specific volume, 481 divided by
0.775, which is about 621 kilopascals, or 6.2 bar. That figure, the constant pressure which acting over the
swept volume would do the same work, is the standard way of comparing engines of different sizes, and real
naturally aspirated petrol engines typically achieve 8 to 12 bar of brake mean effective pressure at their
torque peak.

sections.heading: The Four Strokes in a Real Engine
sections.body:
A real four-stroke engine performs the thermodynamic cycle across two complete revolutions of the crankshaft, or
720 degrees, with one power stroke in that interval. Each cylinder therefore produces useful work for only about
a quarter of the time, which is why multi-cylinder engines and flywheels exist: they smooth the delivery.

The intake stroke begins with the piston at top dead centre and the intake valve open. As the piston descends,
the volume above it grows and the pressure inside falls slightly below the pressure in the intake manifold, so
air, or an air and fuel mixture, flows in. The pressure difference driving this flow is small, typically a few
kilopascals at wide-open throttle, which is why intake port design, valve size and manifold tuning matter so
much. At part throttle, the throttle plate deliberately restricts flow, and the cylinder must be filled against a
manifold vacuum of perhaps 40 to 70 kilopascals absolute. The work spent doing that is pumping loss, and it is
the single largest efficiency penalty a petrol engine pays in ordinary driving.

The compression stroke follows. Both valves close, the piston rises, and the trapped mixture is compressed. This
is the process the ideal cycle models as isentropic, and the real version departs from it in two ways: heat
flows from the hot gas into the cooler cylinder walls, reducing the final temperature, and some mixture escapes
past the piston rings, a leakage called blow-by, typically well under one percent in a healthy engine.

The power stroke, properly the expansion stroke, is where all the useful work is produced. Ignition actually
occurs before top dead centre, and combustion continues past it, so the pressure peak arrives roughly 12 to 18
crank degrees after top dead centre in a well-tuned engine. The expanding gas drives the piston down, the
connecting rod converts that linear motion into rotation, and pressure falls both from expansion and from heat
loss into the walls, which at part load can carry away 25 to 30 percent of the fuel's energy.

The exhaust stroke expels the burned gas. The exhaust valve opens before bottom dead centre, typically 40 to 60
degrees early, so that the still-pressurised gas blows itself out through the port in what is called blowdown.
Sacrificing a little expansion work this way is a net gain, because it means the rising piston does not have to
push against high pressure for the whole stroke. The remaining gas is then swept out, and a small residual
volume of exhaust always stays behind in the clearance space, diluting the next charge.

A useful memory aid, attributed to generations of mechanics, runs suck, squeeze, bang, blow. It is crude, and it
is exactly right.

sections.heading: Valve Timing, Breathing and Volumetric Efficiency
sections.body:
An engine is fundamentally an air pump, and its power output is set almost entirely by how much air it can move,
since the fuel it can usefully burn is fixed by that air. The measure of breathing performance is volumetric
efficiency: the mass of fresh charge actually trapped in the cylinder divided by the mass that would fill the
swept volume at ambient density. A typical naturally aspirated engine achieves 75 to 85 percent at low speed and
85 to 95 percent near its torque peak, while a carefully tuned high-performance engine can exceed 100 percent
over a narrow speed band, and a forced-induction engine can far exceed it because the intake air is denser than
ambient.

Exceeding 100 percent without a compressor is possible because gas has inertia. A column of air moving down an
intake runner does not stop instantly when the piston reaches bottom dead centre, so if the intake valve is held
open past that point, air keeps ramming in. In addition, each valve event sends pressure waves travelling up and
down the runner at the speed of sound, roughly 340 metres per second at ambient temperature and higher when hot.
If runner length is chosen so that a returning positive pressure wave arrives at the valve just before it
closes, it packs additional charge in. Because the arrival timing depends on engine speed, this tuning works
only over a band, which is why variable-length intake manifolds and resonance chambers exist.

Valve timing is therefore never simply open at top dead centre and close at bottom dead centre. The intake valve
typically opens 10 to 25 degrees before top dead centre and closes 40 to 70 degrees after bottom dead centre.
The exhaust valve opens 40 to 60 degrees before bottom dead centre and closes 10 to 20 degrees after top dead
centre. The interval where both are open around top dead centre is called overlap, and it uses the momentum of
the outgoing exhaust to help draw in fresh charge, a scavenging effect. Large overlap improves high-speed
breathing and produces the characteristic lumpy idle of a race camshaft, because at low speed it lets exhaust gas
back into the intake and dilutes the charge.

Late intake valve closing has a further consequence that connects directly back to thermodynamics. If the valve
stays open well past bottom dead centre, some charge is pushed back out, so the effective compression ratio is
lower than the geometric one while the expansion ratio remains full. That deliberate asymmetry is the basis of
the Atkinson and Miller strategies used in hybrid engines.

Variable valve timing systems, which rotate the camshaft relative to the crankshaft hydraulically, let an engine
have both a low-overlap timing for smooth idle and low-speed torque and a high-overlap timing for peak power.
More elaborate systems vary lift and duration as well, allowing throttle-free load control and eliminating much
of the pumping loss.

sections.heading: Ignition, Flame Travel and Spark Advance
sections.body:
The ideal cycle adds heat instantaneously, but combustion in a real engine is a physical process with a duration,
a direction and a speed, and almost every practical problem in spark-ignition engineering comes from that fact.

Ignition begins when the spark plug produces an arc across a gap of typically 0.7 to 1.1 millimetres, at
voltages of 10 to 40 kilovolts, depositing on the order of 30 to 100 millijoules into a tiny volume. That energy
creates a small kernel of burning gas a millimetre or two across. For the first crucial fraction of a millisecond
nothing much appears to happen; this is the ignition delay or flame development period, conventionally taken as
the time to burn the first ten percent of the charge, and it typically occupies 15 to 25 crank degrees.

Once established, the flame front propagates outward through the unburned mixture. A laminar flame in a
stoichiometric petrol and air mixture travels at only about 0.4 to 0.5 metres per second, which would be far too
slow to burn a cylinder's charge in the time available at 3000 revolutions per minute. What saves the engine is
turbulence. The intake process and the piston motion generate large-scale swirl and tumble that break down into
small-scale turbulence near top dead centre, wrinkling and stretching the flame front so that its effective
surface area is many times its apparent area. The resulting turbulent flame speed is on the order of 10 to 30
metres per second, and combustion of the main charge occupies roughly 20 to 40 crank degrees.

Because the total burn takes 40 to 60 degrees, the spark must be fired before top dead centre so that the
pressure peak lands where it does the most good. Firing too early means high pressure develops while the piston
is still rising, so the engine fights itself, torque falls and knock becomes likely. Firing too late means the
gas expands before it has finished burning, wasting energy out of the exhaust. There is an optimum, known as MBT
timing, for minimum advance for best torque, which places the fifty percent burn point at roughly 8 to 10 degrees
after top dead centre and the peak pressure at roughly 12 to 18 degrees after.

Because burn duration in crank degrees is roughly constant while time per degree shrinks with speed, the required
advance grows with revolutions per minute, from perhaps 8 to 15 degrees at idle to 30 to 40 degrees at high
speed with light load. Advance also increases at low load, because a diluted, throttled charge burns more slowly.
Older engines achieved this with centrifugal weights and a vacuum diaphragm on the distributor; modern engines
look the value up in a calibrated map indexed by speed and load, then trim it in real time using feedback from a
knock sensor.

sections.heading: Knock: The Hard Ceiling on Compression
sections.body:
Knock, also called detonation or pinking, is the phenomenon that has limited the compression ratio of petrol
engines for a century, and understanding it explains almost everything about fuel grades.

The mechanism is autoignition of the end gas. As the flame front advances from the spark plug, it compresses the
unburned mixture ahead of it, so that portion of the charge experiences rising pressure and temperature from two
sources at once, the piston and the expanding burned gas. If that end gas reaches conditions where it ignites
spontaneously before the flame arrives, it does not burn progressively but releases its energy almost all at
once, in microseconds, across a substantial volume. The resulting pressure wave travels at well over the speed
of sound in the chamber and reflects off the walls, producing pressure oscillations typically in the 5 to 10
kilohertz range. Those oscillations are what the ear hears as a metallic rattle and what a piezoelectric knock
